clue.text: Congratulations from 121, reportedly

parts.note: said out loud, the figures 121 become 'one to one': congratulations passed from a person back to that same person

explanation.surface: Someone receives congratulations from a mysterious number, or so the story goes.
explanation.walkthrough: '121' looks like a number to look up in the grid, but spoken it is 'one to one', and praise going from one person to that same one is praise of oneself.
explanation.definitionFit: Praise a person heaps on themselves is the same as congratulating oneself, with no outside admirer involved.

clue.text: Strip frame

definitions.meaning: a strip of cloth worn across the body or round the waist
the frame holding the glass panes of a window that slides up and down

explanation.surface: An instruction to take apart a frame.
explanation.definitionFit: A long band of cloth worn over the shoulder is a strip of fabric; the sliding part of a window holding the glass is its frame.

clue.text: Aristocrat has lead lining replaced with gold

indicators.note: says the inner letters of the word for lead are swapped out for a word meaning gold

parts.note: taken as the word itself, whose lining is its inner pair of letters
OR is gold in heraldry

explanation.surface: A nobleman's lead-lined object has been upgraded with gold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lining' means the inside letters of LEAD, which are EA; 'replaced with' puts OR, heraldic gold, in their place.
explanation.definitionFit: A peer of the realm with a title is an aristocrat.

clue.text: Concert party mostly upset society engagements

indicators.note: upset signals that the letters are knocked over into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: mostly means the word for party loses its final letter

parts.note: taken as written, trimmed

explanation.surface: A concert party falls apart, upsetting the engagements of high society.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mostly' trims PARTY to PART; CONCERT plus PART is rearranged by 'upset' into PRECONTRACT, and S for society follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Agreements made in advance, such as betrothals, are commitments or engagements entered into beforehand.

clue.text: Left occupied without leaning

indicators.note: without is used in its old sense of outside, so the word for occupied surrounds the letter

parts.note: AT IT means busy, occupied with something

explanation.surface: Someone left at a loose end, standing upright with no lean.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' here means outside, not lacking: AT IT (busy) goes round L. The surface tempts you to read 'without leaning' as upright.
explanation.definitionFit: Tipped to one side, like a lance held aslant, is the sense of leaning.

clue.text: Harry greets his visitor

indicators.note: to harry is to harass or disturb, so these letters are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: A man named Harry welcomes the person who has come to see him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Harry' reads as a name but is the verb meaning to harass, signalling that GREETS HIS be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A tourist touring the attractions is a kind of visitor.

clue.text: Initially fought in enemy's foreign land

indicators.note: initially tells us to take the opening letter of each of the following words in turn

explanation.surface: A war story: someone first fought in a hostile country abroad.
explanation.definitionFit: In feudal times an estate granted by a lord in return for service was land held from him.

clue.text: They keep cool when ski etc breaks round raised block

indicators.note: round means the rearranged letters go around the other piece
breaks signals that the letters of ski and etc are smashed into a new order
in a down clue, raised means the word is read upwards, so backwards

parts.note: a cube is a solid block

explanation.surface: Skis and other equipment are broken around a block lifted up, keeping things cold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'breaks' rearranges SKI ETC into ICKETS; 'raised' turns CUBE upward in this down entry to EBUC; 'round' wraps ICKETS around it.
explanation.definitionFit: Containers filled with ice for chilling bottles of wine keep drinks cold.

clue.text: Extra income generated by bar

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'Extra income generated by bar' for FRESHENERS: no definition or wordplay found that yields the letters (FRESHERS round EN fits but no clue words give those pieces); searches found no source.

clue.text: Refuse to be blocked by the net?

definitions.meaning: a noun here: the waste matter such as coal dust left behind by sifting

definitions.text: to be blocked by the net?
definitions.meaning: things caught by a mesh screen are what a net stops, which is what screening does

explanation.surface: A footballer refuses to have his shot stopped by the goal net.
explanation.definitionFit: Screenings are the coarse rubbish left after sifting, so they are refuse; and things screened are held back by a mesh, so blocked by a net.

clue.text: Goose seen in Serpentine? Nearly

indicators.note: in tells us the answer sits inside the run of letters across these words

explanation.surface: Was that a goose spotted on the Serpentine lake? Almost.
explanation.walkthrough: The Serpentine is the lake in London's Hyde Park; the letters run across the end of SerpentiNE and the start of NEarly.
explanation.definitionFit: The nene is the Hawaiian goose, a bird species found in Hawaii.

clue.text: In stadium, boxer scrapped with both hands

indicators.note: scrapped hints at a fight, and signals that the letters of the two words are jumbled

explanation.surface: In a stadium, a boxer fought using both fists.
explanation.walkthrough: 'scrapped' looks like it means fought, fitting the boxer, but it is the signal to rearrange STADIUM BOXER.
explanation.definitionFit: A person able to use either hand equally well works with both hands.

clue.text: As traps, linked for bringing round?

definitions.meaning: trap is slang for the mouth, so two traps joined together describe one pressed to another
bringing round means reviving someone who has stopped breathing or fainted

explanation.surface: Mouse traps joined together are used to revive something.
explanation.definitionFit: Traps is slang for mouths, so two joined are lip to lip; and the kiss of life is a method used to revive a casualty.

clue.text: Settled old scores?

parts.note: scores here means pieces of music, and settled old ones are the familiar recurring tunes that open a programme

explanation.surface: Have long-standing grudges finally been avenged?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Settled old scores' suggests revenge, but scores are musical, and settled, familiar ones are a series' signature music.
explanation.definitionFit: The signature music played at the start of a TV or radio programme is a settled, oft-repeated piece of music.

clue.text: Rotten gunge ran so disgustingly

indicators.note: disgustingly signals the letters are churned into a revolting new arrangement

explanation.surface: Foul sludge oozed in a revolting manner from a decaying wound.
explanation.walkthrough: Gunge is British slang for sticky, messy goo.
explanation.definitionFit: Tissue affected by gangrene is decaying flesh, so it is putrid or rotten.

clue.text: Emotional pain from suspect healthcare left wanting

indicators.note: suspect signals that the letters are dubious and need rearranging

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for left, which is missing from the fodder

explanation.surface: Doubtful medical care leaves a patient hurting emotionally.
explanation.walkthrough: 'left wanting' says HEALTHCARE without L; 'suspect' rearranges the remaining nine letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Grief or sorrow felt deeply is emotional pain.

clue.text: Rigorous condition?

parts.note: read as a pun on rigor, the stiffness of body, a state of rigid immobility rather than strictness

explanation.surface: Are these terms strict and demanding?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rigorous' suggests strict; read as rigor (muscle stiffness) plus -ous, it describes a state of being frozen stiff.
explanation.definitionFit: A medical state in which the patient becomes rigid and motionless is a condition marked by stiffness.

clue.text: Joining endless fill

indicators.note: endless means the word for joining loses its first and last letters

parts.note: linking means joining

explanation.surface: Joining a never-ending queue to fill up.
explanation.definitionFit: To complete a drawing by colouring in the outlines is to fill it in.

clue.text: Mum holding big meeting's rock solid? Not quite

indicators.note: holding means the word for mum contains the other piece

parts.note: MA is mother, mum
AGM, annual general meeting, is a big gathering of members

explanation.surface: Mother is hosting a large gathering, and her resolve is almost unshakeable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rock solid' reads as firm resolve, but the definition is molten rock, which is rock but not yet solid.
explanation.definitionFit: Molten material beneath the earth's crust is rock in liquid form, not quite set hard.

clue.text: Annoying type, according to people in high places

indicators.note: in means the people are placed inside the high places

parts.note: tors are rocky hilltops, so two of them are high places
men are people

explanation.surface: A nuisance, as described by those in positions of power.
explanation.walkthrough: 'people in high places' suggests VIPs, but it is MEN placed between two tors, rocky peaks such as those on Dartmoor in England.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who torments others is a pest who deliberately annoys.

clue.text: What's left here repeatedly is clear

indicators.note: repeatedly means the number is written out twice in a row

parts.note: the number printed to the left of this clue in the grid listing is 20

explanation.surface: A puzzle about what remains is obvious.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue points at its own number, 20; repeated, it gives perfect eyesight, which sees clearly.
explanation.definitionFit: Normal sharp eyesight measured as 20/20 vision sees clearly.

clue.text: Essayist's almost caught up

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means the word is read from bottom to top, backwards
almost means the final letter is dropped

parts.note: nailed means caught, as a criminal is

explanation.surface: An essay writer has nearly been caught.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' trims NAILED to NAILE, and 'up' turns that into ELIAN. Elia was the pen name of Charles Lamb, the English essayist.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective formed from Elia, Charles Lamb's pen name, means belonging to that essayist.

clue.text: In The Independent crossword? Hear hear!

indicators.note: the first word tells us to listen to how the next word is pronounced

parts.note: the word hear itself, as said aloud

explanation.surface: A cheer of approval for the newspaper's puzzle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hear hear!' looks like applause, but the first word signals a homophone of the second; the definition is the puzzle being solved now, this place.
explanation.definitionFit: In this very puzzle, the location being pointed at, is this place.

clue.text: Extra amount initially escaping duty

indicators.note: initially escaping means the first letter drops away from the word

parts.note: a bonus is an extra amount paid

explanation.surface: Getting out of a task by paying extra up front.
explanation.definitionFit: A burden or responsibility placed on someone is their obligation or duty.

clue.text: There's no time for unacceptable 12

indicators.note: no here means without, so the letter for time is removed

parts.note: NOT ON is an idiom for unacceptable

explanation.surface: There is no time left for a terrible twelve o'clock.
explanation.definitionFit: Twelve o'clock in the middle of the day is midday.

clue.text: In Australia, point out faculty boss based there?

indicators.note: out signals that the letters of point are put out of order

parts.note: a dean heads a university faculty

explanation.surface: In Australia, someone points out the head of a university department.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' rearranges POINT into NTIPO after A; the definition refers back to Australia, the land on the opposite side of the globe from Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: Antipodean describes things from Australia or New Zealand, the lands on the far side of the globe, so based down under.

clue.text: Indifferent plea for help will attract nothing

parts.note: SOS is the distress signal
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A half-hearted cry for help gets no response.
explanation.definitionFit: Middling, neither good nor bad, is mediocre or indifferent.

clue.text: Unpleasant nastiness surrounding a composer

indicators.note: surrounding means the rearranged letters go round the single letter
unpleasant signals the letters are mangled into a new order

explanation.surface: Nasty unpleasantness surrounds a musician.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unpleasant' rearranges NASTINESS around A to give the French composer Camille Saint-Saëns.
explanation.definitionFit: Camille Saint-Saëns wrote The Carnival of the Animals, making him a French composer.
